title: A Survey of DDoS Attack and Defense Technologies in Multiaccess Edge Computing
researchArea: Multiaccess Edge Computing (MEC) Security / DDoS Attack & Defense Survey
problem: Lack of systematic, architecture-centric surveys evaluating DDoS attack variants (such as Link Flood, Flow-Table Overflow, OpenFlow Agent, and Resource Exhaustion attacks) and defense mechanisms specifically tailored for resource-constrained, multi-tenant Multiaccess Edge Computing (MEC) networks.
motivation: Traditional cloud-centric DDoS defense mechanisms introduce high latency, consume network bandwidth, and fail to address unique edge vulnerabilities (e.g., virtualization deficiencies, coarse-grained access control, and low-rate SDN attacks). A comprehensive synthesis is needed to guide lightweight, adaptive defense design across cloud, edge server, and edge device layers.
noveltyAndContributions: Structured a 3-layer MEC architecture model (Cloud Server Layer, Edge Server Layer, Edge Device Layer) and mapped specific attack surfaces across layers.

Categorized DDoS threats into traditional flooding/slow-request attacks vs. MEC architecture-specific attacks (SDN-targeted LFA/FTO/OpenFlow Agent and server-targeted Resource Exhaustion/Power/Zero-day attacks).

Taxonomized edge defense solutions across multiaccess device network methods (Supervised, Reinforcement, Deep/Federated Learning) and architectural mitigation mechanisms (SDN, Blockchain, NFV, Security Slicing).
Reviewed commercial edge defense case studies (Akamai Kona Site Defender and Cloudflare DDoS Protection) and identified critical open research directions.
methodology: Conducting a comprehensive literature survey, synthesizing, taxonomizing, and systematically comparing over 120 state-of-the-art research papers and industry reports on MEC DDoS security.
Comparing survey taxonomy against prior literature reviews to highlight unique focus areas on lightweight edge server constraints and SDN/MEC integration.
Tabulating comparative analyses of attack variants (by targeted layer, rate, operational impact) and defense mechanisms (by dataset, detection method, application domain, and limitations).
keyAssumptions: MEC networks require defense solutions that operate close to network endpoints (at the Edge Server Layer) to maintain low-latency responsiveness for legitimate traffic while preventing botnet spread.
datasets: Surveyed datasets include: CICDDoS2019, BoT-IoT, CIC-IDS2017, UNSW-NB15, IoT-23, 5G-NIDD, VDoS, InSDN, RT_IoT2022, KDDCUP99, UNB ISCX, Fog IIoT Factory.
experimentalSetup: Literature survey and analytical comparative synthesis (no standalone empirical benchmark setup).
baselines: Prior survey papers: Zargar et al. (2013), Xiao et al. (2019), Zeyu et al. (2020), Ranaweera et al. (2021), Gyamfi & Jurcut (2022), Uddin et al. (2024).
flAlgorithms: Surveyed FL approaches include: FedAvg (weighted parameter aggregation), Collaborative Federated Learning (CFL), Zero-X (Blockchain + Open-Set Recognition FL), and FLEAM (GRU-based FL for IIoT).
xaiEvaluation: Identified the black-box nature and lack of interpretability in deep learning defense models as a key vulnerability, emphasizing the need for transparent decision-making in edge network security.
metrics: Evaluated metrics across surveyed papers: Detection Rate (DR), False Positive Rate (FPR) / False Alarm Rate (FAR), Accuracy, Memory / CPU Overhead, Latency / Response Time (ms), Energy / Power Consumption, Throughput.
results: Synthesized and compared over 60 defense frameworks across traditional and edge-specific categories. Highlighted that combining lightweight traditional statistical methods (e.g., entropy) with adaptive AI (RL/FL) and SDN/P4 data-plane offloading offers the most viable path toward real-time edge protection.
failureConditions: Centralized SDN controllers suffer from CPU exhaustion and flow-table saturation when targeted by low-rate FTO or OpenFlow Agent spoofing attacks.
Pure machine learning/deep learning edge models degrade under zero-day attacks or when trained on outdated, static datasets lacking IoT device diversity.
costEvaluation: Analyzed computational, latency, memory, and energy costs associated with running defense models directly on resource-constrained edge servers vs. offloading detection tasks to the cloud or P4 switches.

limitations.text: Most surveyed machine learning defense methods rely on outdated datasets (KDDCUP99, UNSW-NB15) that lack multiaccess edge device diversity and modern Layer-2/Layer-3 IoT attack vectors.
Current defense frameworks lack standardized service management mechanisms for handling user access offloading, idle resource sharing, or server failover when an edge node is overwhelmed.
limitations.theme: Lack of MEC Service Management Standardization

limitations.text: Advanced decentralized mechanisms (blockchain consensus, proxy re-encryption) introduce high computational overhead and encryption latency, limiting real-time deployment on edge hardware.
limitations.theme: Computational Latency of Blockchain & Crypto Controls

futureWork: Develop multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for collaborative, low-overhead edge server defense.
Advance Federated Learning (FL) frameworks to resolve data non-IIDness and security budget disparities across edge nodes.
Implement P4 data-plane programming to offload complex DDoS filtering policies directly onto switch hardware.
Integrate Security Slicing (5G/ZSM) to isolate malicious traffic streams without disrupting critical edge services.
relevance: Provides moderate/supporting relevance to your thesis by surveying Federated Learning (FL), SDN controllers, and Multiaccess Edge Computing (MEC) defense architectures. Crucially, it highlights ARP Spoofing (D-ARPSpoof) and Layer-2/Layer-3 edge threat vectors alongside OpenFlow domain limitations.
newIdeas: Utilize this survey's taxonomic distinction between SDN control-plane vs. data-plane attacks (LFA, FTO) to evaluate Explainable Federated Learning (XAI + FL) for Layer-2 intrusion detection across heterogeneous edge segments.
